list.listitem: Consider the diagnosis of oral herpes simplex in patients presenting with recurrent, painful vesiculopustules, erosions, ulcers, and crust of the lips and oral cavity. C

Oral herpes simplex is a clinical diagnosis but in cases of uncertainty, polymerase chase reaction (PCR) testing for herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) and HSV-2 of active lesions is an accurate way to confirm diagnosis. B
Consider long-term (>1 month) oral antiviral therapy for patients with recurrent oral herpes simplex, but be aware of its small magnitude of effect balanced by its excellent safety profile. B
Short- and long-term topical therapies are not effective or have insufficient evidence in preventing recurrent oral herpes. B
Oral acyclovir and valacyclovir are effective in treating and preventing herpes simplex infections in patients undergoing cancer treatment. B

background.definition: Oral herpes simplex (herpes simplex labialis, herpetic gingivostomatitis, fever blisters, cold sores) is a mucocutaneous infection caused by HSV-1 and HSV-2. In contrast, recurrent oral herpes simplex is caused primarily by HSV-1.

list.listitem: 62% of adolescents aged 12 to 22 years were seropositive for HSV-1.
HSV-1 and HSV-2
Recurrence may be triggered by fever, stress, menstruation, ultraviolet light exposure, or facial cosmetic surgery.
Herpes labialis is most often caused by HSV-1. Infection is commonly acquired during childhood or adolescence. Incubation period is 2 to 12 days, with the lesion lasting 7 to 10 days.
The virus may become latent, resting in the sensory ganglia with recurrence at or near the original site.
It is spread by direct or indirect contact with infected lesions. Oral-to-genital contact may spread oral herpes to genitalia and vice versa so that it is possible to have HSV-2 on the oral mucosa.
Long-term (>1 month) use of oral antiviral therapy for chronic secondary prevention of recurrent herpes labialis appears effective and safe, albeit with small net clinical benefit. B
Short- and long-term topical therapies are not effective or have insufficient evidence in preventing recurrent oral herpes. B
Oral acyclovir and valacyclovir are effective in preventing herpes simplex infections in patients undergoing cancer treatment. B

Patients undergoing facial cosmetic procedures (i.e., facial resurfacing), those who anticipate intensive exposure to UV light (e.g., skiers or those who work outdoors), and patients with atopic dermatitis are at risk of HSV reactivation and may consider short-term use of oral antiviral therapy. C
Spread of herpes to other skin areas may be prevented by covering and/or minimizing contact with the affected areas. Good hand washing after contact with infected skin should be encouraged. C
Consider the diagnosis of oral herpes simplex in patients presenting with recurrent, painful vesiculopustules, erosions, ulcers, and crusts of the lips and oral cavity. C
Oral herpes simplex is a clinical diagnosis but in cases of uncertainty, PCR testing for HSV-1 and HSV-2 of active lesions is an accurate way to confirm diagnosis. B
HSV viral culture is the gold standard in diagnosing oral herpes simplex (97.1% sensitive, 100% specific), but is rarely necessary. B

Differential.Differential_Features: History of infected contact person, ulcers in the mouth and throat and similar lesions on the feet and hands
History of infected contact person, very small vesicular rash on hands, feet and mouth
Usually found on the movable parts of the mouth, i.e., tongue or the buccal mucosa
Vesicular eruption seen along a dermatome, usually unilateral
History of eczema and/or atopic dermatitis with herpetic infection of skin not oral mucosa
Mainly in children, scarlatiniform erythema with flaccid bullae and erosions that are widespread and life-threatening
Predominantly on face and legs, fiery red appearance (St. Anthony's fire)
Indurated red painful nodules, mostly face, axilla and genital area
history of contact sports; face, neck and shoulder area with herpetic infection
HSV infection of the hand usually involving one or more digits

list.listitem: Diagnosis is usually based on clinical appearance and symptoms of pain (with prodrome for some patients). History of typical factor precipitating the outbreak is also supportive.
Patients may have prodromal symptoms of itching, burning, tingling or hypersensitivity occurring about 2 days prior to the eruption.
Diagnosis is usually based on clinical appearance—clusters of painful vesicles with subsequent erosion and crusting persisting up to 10 days.
The lesions may occur on the lips, buccal mucosa, gingiva, tongue and palate.
Fever, malaise and tender submandibular or cervical lymphadenopathy may be present.
Viral culture of the lesion for HSV is still the gold standard in most labs. In one study, viral culture was 97.1% sensitive and 100% specific for HSV detection.

Nested-polymerase chain reaction (PCR) appears to be more sensitive than cell culture. The sensitivity of cell culture compared to PCR for genital herpes was 46.1% for HSV-1 and 48% for HSV-2 in a STI clinic in Singapore. The specificity of PCR was 100%.

Direct immunofluorescence (DIF) assays provide results in less than one day. In one RCT using viral culture as the gold standard, the sensitivity and specificity of DIF was 88% and 100%, respectively, when indeterminate specimens were excluded. When these were included, the estimated sensitivity ranged from 70% to 90% and the specificity remained at 100%.
Tzanck test of scraping from the lesion may show multinucleated giant cells. This is rarely used given the widespread availability and better accuracy of PCR and immunofluorescence testing.
Suspect herpes labialis in patients with clusters of painful vesicles on the lips or buccal mucosa.
Confirmatory testing is recommended when clinical picture is unclear. The best initial test is PCR testing of active lesions.
Options for treatment of a first episode of oral herpes simplex include acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir started within 48 to 72 hours. C
Antiviral treatment for recurrent episodes of herpes labialis appears effective in reducing time to healing by approximately 1 day. B

For recurrent herpes labialis, treatment with a combination of oral valacyclovir with topical clobetasol appears to be the most effective treatment in terms of reducing time-to-healing and the rate of ulcerative lesions. B
For chronic secondary prevention of recurrent herpes labialis, long-term (>1 month) use of oral acyclovir and famcyclovir appears effective and safe, albeit with small net clinical benefit. B
Oral acyclovir and valacyclovir are effective in treating herpes simplex infections in patients undergoing cancer treatment. B

For treatment of an initial episode of oral herpes simplex, options include acyclovir 400 mg orally three times daily for 7 to 10 days, or valacyclovir 1 gm orally twice daily for 7 to 10 days started within 48 to 72 hours of onset of symptoms. Good trials are lacking, though.
Options for treatment of a recurrent episode include acyclovir 400 mg orally three times daily for 5 days started within 5 hours, valacyclovir, or famciclovir.

Topical steroids used in combination with oral antivirals may be more effective than antiviral monotherapy. A 2023 network meta-analysis compared the efficacy and safety of various antiviral agents for the treatment and prevention of herpes labialis, including 52 articles in the qualitative synthesis. Specifically, 26 articles were analyzed for the primary treatment outcome: time-to-healing. Among the interventions studied, the combination of oral valacyclovir and topical clobetasol was found to be the most effective, with a mean reduction in healing time of -3.50 days (95% CI -5.22 to -1.78). This was followed by vidarabine monophosphate with a mean reduction of -3.22 days (95% CI -4.59 to -1.85), epigallocatechin-3-gallate (the predominant catechin found in green tea) with -2.77 days (95% CI -4.46 to -1.08), famciclovir with -2.09 days (95% CI -2.53 to -1.65), and tetracaine with -2.10 days (95% CI -2.64 to -1.55). Although acyclovir was the most frequently used intervention, it ranked below several other treatments in terms of efficacy, with a mean reduction of -0.92 days (95% CI -1.44 to -0.40). The analysis revealed no significant heterogeneity or publication bias for the time-to-healing (TTH) outcome. Regarding safety, the majority of studies reported either no adverse events or only mild side effects, such as headache, nausea, and application site reactions, indicating a favorable safety profile for the antiviral agents analyzed for the primary outcome. For the primary prevention outcome, only 7 articles met inclusion criteria for analysis, and no intervention was found to be significantly superior. An earlier systematic review and meta-analysis of four RCTs (n=1891) with methodologic limitations demonstrated a significantly lower risk of ulcerative lesions with combination therapy versus antiviral therapy alone (OR 0.73, 95% CI 0.58-0.92, p=0.007).

Monotherapy with oral antivirals has been associated with a reduction in healing time by approximately 1 day in patients with recurrent herpes labialis. A systematic review and meta-analysis of 25 RCTs (n=8453) comparing oral antivirals to placebo demonstrated that antivirals were associated with faster healing time for classic HSV lesions (mean difference: -1.09 days; 95% CI -1.27 to -0.92). This meta-analysis is somewhat limited by heterogeneity and incomplete risk of bias assessment.

For chronic secondary prevention of recurrent herpes labialis, long-term (>1 month) use of oral antiviral therapy appears effective and safe, albeit with small clinical benefit. A Cochrane review found 1 RCT with low-quality evidence showing that oral acyclovir slightly reduced clinical recurrences (1.80 vs 0.85 episodes per participant over 4 months, P=0.009) and virological recurrence (1.40 vs 0.40 per participant over 4 months, P=0.003). One RCT found that long-term valacyclovir reduces the incidence of oral herpes by 0.09 episode per participant per month (n=95), while another RCT found that long-term valacyclovir reduces the incidence of oral herpes better than episodic valacyclovir by 0.10 episode per participant per month (95% CI -0.16 to -0.05; n=120). Moderate-quality evidence from these three trials found similar adverse events between oral antiviral medications and comparator or placebo.

Short-term (≤1 month) use of oral antiviral medications to treat recurrent oral herpes showed inconsistent results. Two RCTs (low-quality evidence) found that oral acyclovir 400 mg twice daily decreased the recurrence rate of oral herpes (RR 0.26, 95% CI 0.13-0.51, n=177). In contrast, one RCT (moderate-quality evidence) evaluating acyclovir 800mg twice daily and 2 RCTs (low-quality evidence) evaluating acyclovir 200 mg five times daily did not demonstrate any preventive efficacy (RR 1.08, 95% CI 0.62-1.87, n=237; RR 0.46, 95% CI 0.20-1.07, n=66, respectively). Furthermore, 1 RCT (moderate-quality evidence) showed uncertain efficacy for the short-term use of valacyclovir to prevent recurrent oral herpes (RR 0.55, 95% CI 0.23-1.28, n=125). So did another RCT for the short-term use of famciclovir.

Oral famciclovir 250 mg three times daily for five days to treat experimental ultraviolet (UV) light-induced herpes simplex labialis decreased mean lesion surface area by more than 50% and accelerated healing time from 5.8 days (placebo subjects) to 3.0 days (medicated group).

One RCT involving 743 adults evaluating docosanol 10% cream applied 5 times daily within 12 hours of symptoms onset resulted in slightly faster healing (4.1 vs 4.8 days, 95% CI 2-22 hours) and slightly faster time to cessation of pain (2.2 vs 2.5 days, 95% CI 3-16 hours) than placebo.

Another RCT involving 2209 patients evaluating penciclovir 1% cream applied every 2 hours while awake resulted in slightly faster healing (4.8 vs 5.5 days, P<0.001) and relief of pain (i.e., mean of 14 hours faster).

Short-term use of topical antiviral medications to prevent recurrent oral herpes does not appear to be effective. Two RCTs (moderate-quality evidence) evaluating topical acyclovir 5% showed no efficacy (pooled RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.48-1.72, n=271). Another RCT (moderate-quality evidence) evaluating topical foscarnet 3% for the prevention of recurrent oral herpes simplex also showed no efficacy (RR 1.08, 95% CI 0.82-1.40, n=295). Topical antiviral agents do not appear to increase adverse events compared to placebo.

Similarly, long-term use of topical antiviral agents for the prevention of recurrent oral herpes has uncertain effectiveness. One RCT evaluating topical acyclovir, compared to placebo, only showed decrease in research-diagnosed recurrences but not participant-reported recurrences. Another RCT failed to show superiority of 1,5 pentanediol gel over placebo over a 26-week period. Moreover, 1 RCT found placebo better than 2-hydroxypropyl-β-cyclo dextrin 20% gel over a 6-month period (P=0.003).

The use of sunscreen has unclear benefits for the prevention of recurrent oral herpes. Two RCTs demonstrated the effectiveness of sunscreen in preventing experimental UV light-induced recurrent oral herpes (pooled RR 0.07, 95% CI 0.01-0.33, n=111). In contrast, one RCT failed to show the efficacy of sunscreen in preventing sunlight-induced oral herpes recurrence. (RR 1.13, 95% CI 0.25-5.06, n=51. No adverse events were reported with the use of sunscreen.
In patients undergoing cancer treatment, oral acyclovir appears effective in treating oral herpes simplex infections. Valacyclovir, at low or high doses, appears similarly effective.

There is insufficient evidence for the efficacy of thymopentin, low-level laser therapy, hypnotherapy, lysine, LongoVital® supplementation, gamma globulin, HSV-1 subunit vaccine, and yellow fever vaccine in preventing of oral herpes simplex.
Topical 2% viscous lidocaine can be used for inside and outside the mouth in small amounts to avoid lidocaine toxicity.

The following treatments are not to be used in the mouth, but may be used externally: (1) cool, moist compresses using tap water or aluminum acetate 1:20 to 1:40 (Burrow's solution, Domeboro, Buluboro) or (2) calamine lotion or similar shake lotion containing alcohol, methanol, and/or phenol applied topically.

When treating recurrent herpes labialis with systemic antivirals such as acyclovir or valacyclovir, therapy should be initiated during the prodrome or at the start of the outbreak and continued 5 days for recurrent episodes and 7 to 10 days for an initial episode.
Patients with disseminated infection (e.g., immunosuppressed patients) require urgent referral and hospitalization for intravenous antiviral therapy and isolation.
Eye involvement (herpes simplex ophthalmicus) requires urgent ophthalmology referral and systemic antiviral therapy. Typicall valacyclovir 1000 mg tid for 10 to 14 days.

Secondary bacterial skin infections may require either topical or oral antibiotic therapy. Mupirocin ointment applied twice daily may be used for secondary impetigo around the mouth. Oral cephalexin is a good alternative for more widespread impetiginization.
Spread to the eye can cause HSV keratitis. Blindness is a rare complication of this.
In a single center case series, 7 of 48 neonates with laboratory proven HSV-1 infection were born to mothers with primary herpes labialis during their pregnancy.
First episode may be more severe and generally affects the inside of the mouth. This can lead to poor oral intake in young children and efforts need to be made to prevent dehydration. C

If untreated in immunocompetent patients, oral herpes simplex usually resolves in 1 to 2 weeks. Patients who are immunosuppressed are at higher risk of dissemination, spread to other areas such as the eye, and more frequent recurrences. C
Advise patients to avoid contact with active lesions and wash hands when contact occurs, and to avoid oral contact with others during an active outbreak. C
